newsitem.title: UK: Experts warn UK law may mean more wrongly jailed.
newsitem.headline: Experts warn UK law may mean more wrongly jailed.

text.p: Prominent English lawyers warned on Thursday that a new law on disclosure of evidence to the defence could mean new miscarriages of justice in a country already hit by scandals over people wrongly jailed.

Defence lawyer Jim Nichol complained that under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act, which comes into force on Tuesday giving police and prosecution discretion on disclosing evidence to the defence, crucial information may not be provided.

"It is a recipe for miscarriages of justice," said Nichol, the lawyer for the Bridgewater Three who were falsely jailed for life for killing a 13-year-old boy in 1979 and spent 18 years in prison until their release last month.

He told a news conference to launch "Active Defence", a lawyer's guide to evidence disclosure, that he feared defence lawyers would be blamed for not uncovering evidence that should have been provided by police or prosecutors.
"It is not a level playing field," he said, adding that police investigating a case may not be aware of what is vital to the defence.
Dr Eric Shepherd, a forensic psychologist and co-author of the guide, said it was bizarre to expect police to make decisions for the defence.
Guide co-author Roger Ede said police often regarded probing by the defence as an unnecessary nuisance.

"The ability of defence solicitors to be able to assess the evidence collected by the police, including the evidence that the prosecution has decided not to use, is a vital safeguard in our criminal justice system," he said.
"The government has not learnt any lessons from the miscarriages of justice which came about because of the non-disclosure of evidence, and history will repeat itself," he added.

The Bridgewater case is the latest in a series of miscarriages of justice in England. Michael Hickey, his cousin Vincent Hickey and James Robinson walked free after after an appeal court ruled that their 1979 conviction was unsafe.

Legal experts said if access to police notebooks and information about fingerprints found at the scene of the crime had been available to the defence at the time of the original trial the miscarriage of justice might never have happened.
The "Guildford Four" and "Birmingham Six" were released from long prison sentences after being wrongly convicted of Irish Republican Army bombings on pubs that killed 36 people.
Home Secretary (Interior Minister) Michael Howard, who is noted for his tough stances in fighting crime, says the reforms are needed to help prevent guilty people from escaping justice.
